glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Faith takes God at His word and lives now in light of what He has promised but not yet shown, as the long line of witnesses from Abel to the suffering prophets proves, all of them commended by God and waiting for a fulfillment they will share with us.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 11 answers the call of 10:38–39 to live by faith and not draw back. Its examples come from Genesis through the prophets, and the chapter leads straight into the call to run the race looking to Jesus (12:1–2).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.” (Hebrews 11:1)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Hebrews 11 opens by describing faith: “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (11:1). Faith rests on who God is and what He has said, so His unseen promises carry real weight in how His people live now. It begins with creation itself, understanding that “the worlds were framed by the word of God” (11:3). Then, “without faith it is impossible to please Him,” for whoever comes to God must believe “that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him” (11:6).

The chapter then calls its witnesses. Abel worshiped, Enoch pleased God, and Noah built an ark for a flood no one had seen. Abraham “went out, not knowing where he was going” (11:8), and lived in tents while waiting “for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (11:10). Sarah “judged Him faithful who had promised” (11:11). Abraham offered Isaac, trusting that God could raise him from the dead. Moses chose to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy Egypt’s treasures, “for he endured as seeing Him who is invisible” (11:27). Israel crossed the sea, Jericho’s walls fell, and Rahab was spared.

Many of these people “died in faith, not having received the promises” (11:13). They called themselves strangers and pilgrims, longing for a heavenly country, “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God” (11:16). The chapter honors the same trust in God under very different outcomes. Some through faith conquered kingdoms and escaped the sword; others were tortured, refusing release, “that they might obtain a better resurrection” (11:35). The world was not worthy of them. All were commended, and God has planned for them to be made perfect together with us (11:39–40).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 11:1–3 — What Faith Is

Faith is confident assurance of what God has promised and conviction about realities not yet seen. By faith God’s people of old were commended, and by faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of visible things.

Hebrews 11:4–7 — Abel, Enoch, and Noah

By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice, Enoch was taken without seeing death, and Noah built an ark in response to God’s warning about things not yet seen. Without faith no one can please God, for those who come to Him must believe that He exists and rewards those who seek Him.

Hebrews 11:8–12 — Abraham and Sarah Trust the One Who Promised

By faith Abraham left home without knowing where he was going and lived as a foreigner in the promised land, waiting for the city God Himself would build. By faith Sarah received strength to bear a child in old age because she trusted God’s faithfulness, and from one aging man came countless descendants.

Hebrews 11:13–16 — Strangers Seeking a Heavenly Country

The patriarchs died still trusting God’s promises, seeing them from a distance and confessing that they were strangers on the earth. They longed for a better, heavenly homeland, so God is not ashamed to be called their God and has prepared a city for them.

Hebrews 11:17–22 — Faith That Looks Beyond Death

By faith Abraham offered Isaac, the son of promise, reasoning that God could raise him from the dead, and in a figurative sense he received him back. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph each acted on God’s promises about the future even as they faced death.

Hebrews 11:23–28 — The Faith of Moses

By faith Moses’ parents hid him without fear of the king, and Moses chose to suffer with God’s people instead of enjoying Egypt’s treasures, valuing the reproach of Christ above them. By faith he left Egypt, persevering as one who saw the invisible God, and kept the Passover.

Hebrews 11:29–31 — The Red Sea, Jericho, and Rahab

By faith Israel crossed the Red Sea on dry land, while the pursuing Egyptians drowned. By faith Jericho’s walls fell, and Rahab was spared because she welcomed the spies in peace.

Hebrews 11:32–38 — Faith in Deliverance and in Suffering

The writer has no time to tell of all the judges, kings, and prophets who through faith conquered, escaped danger, and grew strong out of weakness. Others through faith endured torture, chains, and death, refusing release to gain a better resurrection, and the world was not worthy of them.

Hebrews 11:39–40 — Made Perfect Together

All these were commended for their faith, yet they did not receive the promise in its fullness. God planned something better, so that they would reach the goal together with us.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 11 shows that faith is not wishful thinking. It rests on God’s character and His word, and it acts before the outcome can be seen. Abraham went, Noah built, Moses chose, and each trusted that God would keep His promise (11:6–8, 24–26).

The chapter also refuses to measure faith by outcomes alone. Some believers escaped the sword, and others died by it; both are listed as people of faith, and God commends them all (11:33–39). Believers who are suffering are not failing in faith. They stand in the same line as those of whom the world was not worthy, waiting with them for what God has promised.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
What faith is. Faith gives God’s unseen promises real weight now (11:1–3).

Pleasing God. Without faith it is impossible to please Him (11:6).

Pilgrims seeking a city. The patriarchs lived as strangers, waiting for the city God built (11:9–16).

Faith beyond death. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph trusted God’s promises beyond their own lifetimes (11:17–22).

Deliverance and suffering. The same trust in God brought some through to victory and carried others through suffering and death, and God commended it in both (11:32–40).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Faith (11:1). Faith is the persuasion that God is who He has revealed Himself to be in His Word and that He is faithful to perform all He has promised. In this chapter that persuasion shows itself in trust and obedience before the promise can be seen.

Substance and evidence (11:1). Faith gives firm reality to what God has promised and treats unseen things as certain, because God has spoken.

The elders (11:2). God’s people of earlier generations, whom God commended for their faith.

Strangers and pilgrims (11:13). People living away from their true home. The patriarchs confessed that their homeland lay ahead, in the heavenly country God had prepared.

The reproach of Christ (11:26). The disgrace Moses accepted by siding with God’s people. Hebrews counts that suffering as sharing in the reproach Christ Himself would bear.

Made perfect apart from us (11:40). Brought to God’s intended goal. The faithful of old will share that fulfillment together with believers today through Christ.

focus: Hebrews 11 answers the call to live by faith (Hebrews 10:38–39) by showing what faith is and how it has lived through the generations, from Abel to the prophets and the unnamed faithful who suffered. The witnesses act on what God has said before they can see the outcome, and the chapter closes by joining their hope to ours in the fulfillment God has provided for His people together.

sections.title: What Faith Is
sections.summary: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1): faith is firm assurance grounded in what God has promised, and it gives His unseen future real weight in present obedience and endurance. By faith the elders obtained a good testimony, and by faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made of things which are visible.

sections.title: Abel, Enoch, and Noah
sections.summary: By faith Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, and Noah, divinely warned of things not yet seen, prepared an ark for the saving of his household. Between these examples stands the principle that “without faith it is impossible to please Him” (Hebrews 11:6), for whoever comes to God must believe that He is and that He rewards those who diligently seek Him.

sections.title: Abraham and Sarah Trust the One Who Promised
sections.summary: By faith Abraham obeyed and went out, not knowing where he was going, and lived in tents in the land of promise, waiting for “the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10). By faith Sarah received strength to conceive when she was past the age, because she judged Him faithful who had promised, and from one man, as good as dead, came descendants as many as the stars of the sky.

sections.title: Strangers Seeking a Heavenly Country
sections.summary: These all died in faith without receiving the promises, having seen them afar off and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. They desired a better, heavenly country, and so “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them” (Hebrews 11:16).

sections.title: Faith That Looks Beyond Death
sections.summary: By faith Abraham offered up Isaac, the son of promise, concluding that God was able to raise him up even from the dead, from which he also received him in a figurative sense. By faith Isaac and Jacob blessed their descendants concerning things to come, and Joseph, when he was dying, spoke of Israel’s departure and gave instructions concerning his bones.

sections.title: The Faith of Moses
sections.summary: By faith Moses’ parents hid him without fearing the king’s command, and Moses himself refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing affliction with God’s people and “esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt” (Hebrews 11:26). By faith he forsook Egypt, enduring “as seeing Him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27), and kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood.

sections.title: The Red Sea, Jericho, and Rahab
sections.summary: By faith Israel passed through the Red Sea as by dry land, while the Egyptians who attempted it were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they were encircled for seven days, and Rahab did not perish with those who did not believe, because she had received the spies with peace.

sections.title: Faith in Deliverance and in Suffering
sections.summary: Time would fail to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith subdued kingdoms and escaped the edge of the sword, while women received their dead raised to life again. Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, “that they might obtain a better resurrection” (Hebrews 11:35), and still others endured mockings, chains, stoning, the sword, and destitution, people “of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:38).

sections.title: Made Perfect Together
sections.summary: All these obtained a good testimony through faith, yet did not receive the promise in its fullness, even though some had received particular promises along the way (Hebrews 11:17, Hebrews 11:33). God had provided something better for us, the fulfillment He brings to all His people together through Christ, “that they should not be made perfect apart from us” (Hebrews 11:40).

1.brief: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.” Faith trusts God for who He has revealed Himself to be in His Word, and because it rests on His character and promises, it gives the things hoped for and His unseen future real weight in how believers live now.
1.explain:
“the substance of things hoped for” Faith trusts in who God has revealed Himself to be in His word. Because His character and promise are sure, the future He promises has real weight in the present.

“the evidence of things not seen” Faith gives conviction about what remains unseen because it takes God at His word. The examples that follow show that conviction in worship, choices, obedience, suffering, and endurance.
1.notes: The Greek word translated substance here is hypostasis. In Hebrews 1:3 it refers to God’s own being, while in Hebrews 3:14 it is translated confidence. Here it carries the assurance that gives what is hoped for a firm footing in the present.

2.brief: By faith “the elders obtained a good testimony.” The people of old received God’s approval because they trusted Him.
2.explain: “the elders obtained a good testimony” The people of old received God’s commendation through faith. Their testimony is the approval He gave them for trusting Him, which the following examples show in different forms.

3.brief: By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that the things which are seen “were not made of things which are visible.” Faith accepts God’s word as the source of everything that exists, and the word that made the world can be trusted for what He promises.
3.explain: “the worlds were framed by the word of God” The created order owes its existence to God’s spoken word. What we see did not come from visible things. Faith receives God’s account of the unseen beginning and thus recognizes the power of the word on which its hope rests.

4.brief: By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain’s, and God testified that he was righteous by accepting his gifts. Though Abel died, “through it he being dead still speaks,” for his faith still bears witness.
4.explain: “God testifying of his gifts” Abel’s offering was more excellent than Cain’s, and the verse gives faith as the reason. God’s acceptance testified that Abel was righteous. Though he died, his offering still bears witness to faith expressed in worship.

5.brief: By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, “and was not found, because God had taken him.” Before God took him, Enoch had already received the testimony that he pleased God.
5.explain: “he did not see death” God took Enoch so that he could not be found, as Genesis 5:24 records. Before being taken he had already received the testimony that he pleased God. The next verse explains why Hebrews reads that testimony as evidence of faith.

6.brief: “But without faith it is impossible to please Him, for he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him.” Drawing near to God requires trusting that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.
6.explain: “without faith it is impossible to please Him” Coming to God involves believing that He is and trusting His character as the One who rewards those who seek Him earnestly. The verse speaks of faith as the ground of approach to God. Enoch’s life shows how God commends such trust.

7.brief: By faith Noah, warned by God about things not yet seen, “moved with godly fear, prepared an ark for the saving of his household.” Noah’s obedience to God’s warning exposed the unbelief of the world around him, and he became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
7.explain: “being divinely warned of things not yet seen” Noah took God’s warning seriously enough to build the ark while the disaster was still unseen. His reverent obedience saved his household and exposed the world’s unbelief. He became an heir of the righteousness associated with faith.

8.brief: By faith Abraham obeyed when God called him to go to a place he would receive as an inheritance, “And he went out, not knowing where he was going.” Abraham acted on God’s word before he could see where it would lead.
8.explain: “he went out, not knowing where he was going” God called Abraham to leave and go toward an inheritance. Abraham knew the God who called even though he did not know the destination. His departure shows what faith does when God’s command is clear and the outcome remains unseen.

9.brief: By faith Abraham lived in the land of promise as if it were a foreign country, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, “the heirs with him of the same promise.” He lived as a temporary resident in the very land God had promised him.
9.explain: “as in a foreign country” Abraham lived in tents in the very land God promised. Isaac and Jacob shared the promise but also lived there without permanent possession. Their lives show the difference between receiving God’s word and having all that word promises already in hand.

10.brief: Abraham lived in tents as a temporary resident because he was waiting “for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God.” His hope looked beyond tents to a lasting city that God Himself would build.
10.explain: “the city which has foundations” Abraham could live in tents because he was waiting for a lasting city. God designs and builds that city. Its sure foundation explains why Abraham’s hope extended beyond what he owned in the land.

11.brief: By faith Sarah received strength to conceive and bore a child when she was past the age, “because she judged Him faithful who had promised.” She trusted God’s faithfulness when nature said it was impossible.
11.explain: “she judged Him faithful who had promised” Sarah received strength to conceive when she was past the age for bearing children. Her faith was a judgment about God: she counted the One who promised sufficiently faithful to do what He said.

12.brief: From Abraham, one man, and him “as good as dead,” came descendants as many as the stars of the sky and as countless as the sand by the seashore. God’s promise produced abundant life where human strength had failed.
12.explain: “from one man, and him as good as dead” Abraham seemed beyond the natural possibility of fathering the promised family. The stars and the sand picture the multitude God brought from one man. Their number gives visible scale to the faithfulness Sarah counted on.

13.brief: Abraham, Sarah, and the patriarchs “all died in faith, not having received the promises,” yet they saw them from afar, were assured of them, embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. They kept trusting God’s promise even though its fullness lay beyond their lifetimes.
13.explain: “died in faith” The patriarchal family received real beginnings of fulfillment, yet the promises in their fullness lay beyond their lives. They saw the promises from afar, welcomed them, and openly acknowledged their position as strangers and travelers on earth. Death did not undo their trust in the God who had spoken.

14.brief: By calling themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth, the patriarchs made it plain that they were seeking a homeland. That confession showed that their true home still lay ahead of them.
14.explain: “they seek a homeland” Calling themselves strangers and pilgrims expressed more than the fact that they lived in tents. It showed that they were looking for a home ahead of them. Their confession gives the writer reason to ask what country they truly desired.

15.brief: If the patriarchs had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had the opportunity to return. Their homeland was not behind them, and they did not turn back.
15.explain: “they would have had opportunity to return” The country the patriarchs had left lay behind them and was still a place they could have returned to. Their persistent life as travelers shows that the homeland they sought was elsewhere.

16.brief: Instead the patriarchs desired “a better, that is, a heavenly country,” and so God is not ashamed to be called their God, “for He has prepared a city for them.” God gladly identifies Himself with those who long for His heavenly home.
16.explain: “a better, that is, a heavenly country” Their desire was for the country God would provide. He is willing to be called their God and has prepared a city for them. Their trust belonged to a relationship God openly owns and a future He Himself provides.

17.brief: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and the man “who had received the promises offered up his only begotten son.” The test was severe because Isaac was the son through whom God’s promises were to be fulfilled.
17.explain: “Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac” The test in Genesis 22 put Abraham’s obedience alongside the promise he had received. Isaac was the unique son of promise. Abraham yielded him to God, though the promise depended on this very son for its fulfillment.

18.brief: God had said of Isaac, “In Isaac your seed shall be called,” meaning that the descendants God promised Abraham would come through Isaac. That promise made the test so costly, and it explains why Abraham trusted that God could raise Isaac from the dead.
18.explain: “In Isaac your seed shall be called” God had expressly said that Abraham’s promised line would come through Isaac (Genesis 21:12). Abraham therefore had specific words from God to hold as he faced the apparent contradiction between the promise and the command.

19.brief: Abraham concluded “that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead,” and in a figurative sense he did receive Isaac back from the dead. Abraham’s trust rested on God’s power to raise the dead and keep His word.
19.explain: “God was able to raise him up, even from the dead” Abraham trusted God’s power to keep His word even beyond death. Isaac was spared when he had been given up to death in Abraham’s purpose. Hebrews calls that recovery figurative, a return as from death.

20.brief: By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau “concerning things to come.” His blessing looked ahead to God’s future purposes for his sons.
20.explain: “concerning things to come” Isaac’s blessings over Jacob and Esau pointed to futures beyond what he could see. By speaking blessing about what lay ahead, Isaac showed trust that God’s promises reached beyond his own life.

21.brief: By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped, “leaning on the top of his staff.” Even at the end of his life Jacob trusted God’s promise and worshiped Him.
21.explain: “blessed each of the sons of Joseph” At the end of his life Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons and worshiped while leaning on his staff. He still looked to God for the future of the family. His physical weakness did not remove the confidence with which he blessed them.

22.brief: By faith Joseph, when he was dying, spoke of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt and gave instructions concerning his bones. He was so sure of God’s promise that he arranged for his remains to go with Israel to the promised land.
22.explain: “gave instructions concerning his bones” Joseph spoke of Israel’s future departure from Egypt before the people had left. He directed that his remains go with them. That instruction placed his own burial within the future he expected because of God’s promise.

23.brief: By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw he was a beautiful child, “and they were not afraid of the king’s command.” Their trust in God overcame their fear of Pharaoh’s order.
23.explain: “they were not afraid of the king’s command” Moses’ parents saw their child’s beauty and hid him for three months despite Pharaoh’s order. Their faith took the form of protecting him when obedience to the ruler would have cost his life.

24.brief: By faith Moses, when he became of age, “refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.” He gave up his place in Egypt’s royal household.
24.explain: “refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter” When Moses grew up he refused the standing available through Pharaoh’s household. The choice put his identity in question, and the next verse tells us with whom he chose to stand.

25.brief: Moses chose “rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin.” He valued belonging to God’s people above comfort that would not last.
25.explain: “to suffer affliction with the people of God” Moses chose to share the real suffering of God’s people. Egypt could offer the pleasures and advantages of his position, but those would pass. Faith gave him reason to value belonging to God’s people more highly.

26.brief: Moses esteemed “the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt,” for he looked to the reward. Hebrews counts the disgrace he accepted with God’s people as sharing in the reproach of Christ, and he endured it because he valued God’s reward more than Egypt’s wealth.
26.explain: “the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt” Hebrews sees Moses’ willingness to bear shame with God’s people as sharing in the reproach associated with Christ. Moses made his choice in the setting of Israel’s affliction, and Hebrews names its fuller significance. The reward he expected from God made Egypt’s treasure a lesser gain.

27.brief: By faith Moses forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king, “for he endured as seeing Him who is invisible.” His steady awareness of the unseen God gave him courage to persevere.
27.explain: “as seeing Him who is invisible” Moses endured because the unseen God was real to him. Pharaoh’s anger was visible and formidable, but awareness of God gave Moses the courage to leave Egypt and keep going.
27.notes: Readers differ over whether this departure is the earlier flight in Exodus 2 or Moses’ later departure with Israel. Hebrews stresses what enabled him to endure rather than specifying which scene supplies every detail.

28.brief: By faith Moses kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, “lest he who destroyed the firstborn should touch them.” He obeyed God’s instructions and trusted God to protect the households marked with blood.
28.explain: “the Passover and the sprinkling of blood” Moses obeyed the instructions of Exodus 12 and trusted God to spare the households marked with blood. The death of the firstborn was the danger, and following God’s word gave Israel the protection He promised.

29.brief: By faith the Israelites passed through the Red Sea as by dry land, “whereas the Egyptians, attempting to do so, were drowned.” Israel crossed trusting God’s word, and the same sea that opened for them closed over the pursuing Egyptians.
29.explain: “they passed through the Red Sea as by dry land” Israel trusted God’s provision of a way where no way ordinarily existed. The Egyptians attempted the crossing and drowned. The same waters mark God’s rescue for Israel and the end of the pursuing army.

30.brief: By faith “the walls of Jericho fell down after they were encircled for seven days.” God brought down the walls of the fortified city as Israel followed His unusual instructions.
30.explain: “after they were encircled for seven days” Israel obeyed God’s instructions to go around Jericho before any collapse could be seen. God made the walls fall after the completed circuit of days. The victory came in the course of trust expressed as obedience.

31.brief: By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with those who did not believe, “when she had received the spies with peace.” A Canaanite woman’s faith brought her into safety among God’s people.
31.explain: “she had received the spies with peace” Rahab welcomed Israel’s spies because she took seriously what she knew of the LORD (Joshua 2:9–11). Her action set her apart from those who refused to believe, and she survived the judgment that fell on the city.

32.brief: “And what more shall I say?” the writer asks, for time would fail him to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. The line of faith is far longer than he can describe.
32.explain: “the time would fail me to tell” The writer names judges, kings, and prophets without retelling each life. The list widens the witness beyond the people already described and makes room for what faith accomplished in widely differing circumstances.

33.brief: Through faith these people “subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions.” Faith brought victories, just rule, the fulfillment of promises, and rescue from danger.
33.explain: “subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises” Faith was active in public victories, just deeds, the reception of things God promised, and deliverance from terrible danger. The phrase about lions gives a vivid instance of that last kind of rescue. Particular promises were received during life even though the promise in its fullness still lay ahead.

34.brief: Through faith they “quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, became valiant in battle, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.” God’s strength worked through people who trusted Him in their weakness.
34.explain: “out of weakness were made strong” Some escaped fire and sword, and others received strength to prevail in battle and turn hostile armies away. The change from weakness to strength shows how God’s help came in circumstances where His people had little strength of their own.

35.brief: Women “received their dead raised to life again,” while others were tortured and refused release “that they might obtain a better resurrection.” The women received their loved ones back for this life, but those who refused release looked ahead to resurrection into lasting life, and both are instances of faith.
35.explain: “that they might obtain a better resurrection” Some women received their loved ones back into this life. Others refused release from torture because they looked for resurrection into lasting life. Both responses belong in the testimony of faith, and the contrast explains why those who suffered could endure without rescue.

36.brief: Still others endured mocking and whipping, and even chains and imprisonment. Faithfulness to God often led to shame and confinement.
36.explain: “of chains and imprisonment” Faithful people endured ridicule, whipping, and confinement. Hebrews includes these trials just after miraculous deliverances so the congregation will recognize God’s commendation in endurance as well as escape.

37.brief: Some were stoned, sawn in two, tempted, and killed with the sword, while others wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, and tormented. Hebrews honors those whose faith led them to suffering and death.
37.explain: “being destitute, afflicted, tormented” Some were killed, while others survived as wanderers in rough clothing, deprived of shelter and means. The list makes the cost of staying faithful unmistakable. These lives remain part of the same witness as those who prevailed in battle.

38.brief: The world “was not worthy” of these people who wandered in deserts and mountains and lived in dens and caves of the earth. Those the world rejected were people of greater worth than the world that cast them out.
38.explain: “of whom the world was not worthy” The writer reverses the world’s judgment of those it drove into deserts, mountains, dens, and caves. Their rejection did not diminish their worth before God. Hebrews honors precisely the people a hostile society treated as expendable.

39.brief: All these “obtained a good testimony through faith,” yet they “did not receive the promise” in its fullness. God commended their faith even though the complete fulfillment still lay ahead.
39.explain: “having obtained a good testimony through faith” God commended all these people even though the promise had not reached its full fulfillment in their lifetimes. The statement returns to verse 2 and gathers the whole chapter under God’s approval. Waiting remained part of their faith.

40.brief: God had provided “something better for us, that they should not be made perfect apart from us.” The faithful of old will share with believers today in the full fulfillment God brings to His people together through Christ.
40.explain: “they should not be made perfect apart from us” God provided the better fulfillment through Christ so that the faithful of old and believers now reach His intended goal together. Their hope and ours belong to one saving purpose. That shared inheritance prepares for the call to run with our eyes fixed on Jesus.
